title: Ἀνὴρ φέναξ
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 55 (= Perry 28). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἀνὴρ πένης νοσῶν καὶ κακῶς διακείμενος ηὔξατο τοῖς θεοῖς ἑκατὸν βόας τελέσειν, εἰ περισώσειαν αὐτόν.
sentences.tr: Anēr penēs nosōn kai kakōs diakeimenos ēuxato tois theois hekaton boas telesein, ei perisōseian auton.
sentences.l: A poor man, being sick and in a bad way, vowed to the gods that he would offer a hundred oxen, if they should bring him safely through.
sentences.i: A poor man who was ill and in a bad way vowed to the gods that he would sacrifice a hundred oxen if they brought him through.
sentences.n: εὔχομαι with the future infinitive τελέσειν is the regular shape of a vow: 'he vowed that he would perform'. A hundred oxen is a hecatomb, the largest of ordinary offerings and far past a poor man's means — which is the whole of what follows. εἰ περισώσειαν is an optative, the condition as he put it.

sentences.t: Οἱ δὲ ἀπόπειραν αὐτοῦ ποιήσασθαι βουλόμενοι ῥαΐσαι τάχιστα αὐτὸν παρεσκεύασαν.
sentences.tr: Hoi de apopeiran autou poiēsasthai boulomenoi rhaïsai tachista auton pareskeuasan.
sentences.l: And they, wishing to make trial of him, brought it about that he recovered very quickly.
sentences.i: The gods, wishing to put him to the test, had him recover with all speed.
sentences.n: οἱ δέ, 'and they', with the bare article standing for the pronoun. παρασκευάζω with an infinitive is 'to bring it about that…'. ἀπόπειραν ποιήσασθαι takes the genitive of the person tested.

sentences.t: Κἀκεῖνος ἐξαναστάς, ἐπειδὴ ἀληθινῶν βοῶν ἠπόρει, στεατίνους ἑκατὸν πλάσας ἐπί τινος βωμοῦ κατέκαυσεν εἰπών· « Ἀπέχετε τὴν εὐχήν, ὦ δαίμονες. »
sentences.tr: Kakeinos exanastas, epeidē alēthinōn boōn ēporei, steatinous hekaton plasas epi tinos bōmou katekausen eipōn· « Apechete tēn euchēn, ō daimones. »
sentences.l: And he, having got up, since he was at a loss for real oxen, having moulded a hundred of tallow, burnt them on some altar, saying: « Receive the vow in full, you divine powers. »
sentences.i: And once on his feet again, being short of real oxen, he moulded a hundred out of tallow, burned them on an altar, and said: « Take the vow in full, you powers. »
sentences.n: Κἀκεῖνος is crasis, καὶ ἐκεῖνος run into one word. ἀπορέω takes the genitive of what one lacks. ἀπέχετε is the word of the receipt — 'you have it, paid in full' — put into the form of a prayer. Modelled cakes and figures really were offered in place of animals by those who could not afford the beasts, so the swindle wears the dress of ordinary piety.

sentences.t: Οἱ δὲ θεοὶ βουλόμενοι αὐτὸν ἐν μέρει ἀντιβουκολῆσαι ὄναρ αὐτῷ ἔπεμψαν, παραινοῦντες ἐλθεῖν εἰς τὸν αἰγιαλόν· ἐκεῖ γὰρ αὐτὸν εὑρήσειν ἀττικὰς χιλίας.
sentences.tr: Hoi de theoi boulomenoi auton en merei antiboukolēsai onar autōi epempsan, parainountes elthein eis ton aigialon· ekei gar auton heurēsein attikas chilias.
sentences.l: And the gods, wishing to hoax him back in their turn, sent him a dream, urging him to go to the shore; for there, they said, he would find a thousand Attic drachmas.
sentences.n: ἀντιβουκολῆσαι, 'to cheat in return', keeps the ox in it: βουκολέω is to herd cattle and so to lead a man by the nose — a play on the hundred oxen. παραινοῦντες is plural and agrees with οἱ θεοί: it is the gods who urge, through the dream. The last clause slips into accusative and infinitive, still reporting their message. ἀττικὰς χιλίας leaves δραχμάς unexpressed, as a familiar coin regularly is.

sentences.t: Καὶ ὃς περιχαρὴς γενόμενος δρομαῖος ἧκεν ἐπὶ τὴν ἠιόνα.
sentences.tr: Kai hos pericharēs genomenos dromaios hēken epi tēn ēiona.
sentences.l: And he, having become overjoyed, came at a run to the beach.
sentences.i: Overjoyed, he ran down to the shore.
sentences.n: καὶ ὅς, 'and he', is the old use of the relative as a demonstrative, kept alive in narrative. δρομαῖος is an adjective doing adverbial work, 'at a run'.

sentences.t: Ἔνθα δὴ λῃσταῖς περιπεσὼν ἀπήχθη, καὶ ὑπ’ αὐτῶν πωλούμενος εὗρε δράχμας χιλίας.
sentences.tr: Entha dē lēistais peripesōn apēchthē, kai hyp' autōn pōloumenos heure drachmas chilias.
sentences.l: There indeed, having fallen in with pirates, he was carried off, and being sold by them he found a thousand drachmas.
sentences.i: There he fell in with pirates and was carried off, and when they sold him he fetched a thousand drachmas.
sentences.n: εὗρε is the same verb the gods' message used, 'find', but of a price it means 'fetch' — the promise comes true in the worst way. περιπίπτω takes the dative, 'to fall in with'. Seizure by brigands and sale into slavery were an ordinary hazard of the Greek coast.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος εὔκαιρος πρὸς ἄνδρα ψευδολόγον.
sentences.tr: Ho logos eukairos pros andra pseudologon.
sentences.l: Against a man who speaks falsely the story is well-timed.
sentences.n: A closing formula of its own kind, met elsewhere in the collection: not 'the story shows that…' but a note of the occasion on which the fable is aptly told, πρός with the accusative, 'with a view to, against'. The copula ἐστι is left unexpressed, as Greek regularly leaves it.
